view: Yaṣṭarikhūn means crying aloud and calling for help; ṣarākh is a shout, a ṣārikh may be the caller, and a muṣrikh the helper. A poetic example depicts a frightened caller.
The verb is an intensive iftiʿāl form of ṣarākh: its original tāʾ becomes emphatic ṭāʾ near ṣād, making an effortful, forceful cry.
Their screaming in Hell conveys intense suffering and helplessness; the plea that follows explains what they cry out for.
They seek rescue from God, rather than calling to one another in confusion.
Their cries obtain no relief: the punishment is not eased before or after they ask.
They ask God to take them out of Hell and return them to worldly life for another chance to act well.

words: نَعْمَلْ صَٰلِحًا غَيْرَ ٱلَّذِى كُنَّا نَعْمَلُ
view: They promise faith and obedience in place of their former disbelief, polytheism, and disobedience; this includes obeying the messengers, and faith is prerequisite for accepted deeds.
Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the promised righteous deed specifically as professing that there is no god but God.
The added phrase admits former deeds were wrong and heightens regret. It may imply they had wrongly considered their earlier conduct righteous or followed whim and opposition.
Their promise is belated repentance after seeing Resurrection and judgment; their hope for reprieve has become a plea and then a vow to reform.
The rejected request shows their suffering is punishment rather than correction; repentance and repair belong to worldly life, and return from the afterlife is impossible.
Even if returned to the world, they would repeat the forbidden acts; God therefore rejects their request.
Their unqualified promise to do good omits dependence on God and betrays reliance on their own power.

Unlike believers who credit divine grace and see their works as small beside God's blessings, the condemned ask to return and work while failing to recognize the majesty that makes their proposed deeds inadequate.
Their plea belongs to the Qurʾānic accounts of the damned asking for another chance and may form part of an extended exchange with God; their speech precedes the command in 23:108 to stop speaking.
An omitted verb of saying introduces 'Our Lord'; the plea may explain their cries, be independent speech, or describe their state circumstantially.
The jussive verb expresses the result of the request: if You release us, we will do righteous work.
Ṣāliḥan and ghayra may both qualify omitted nouns, or ṣāliḥan may qualify an omitted verbal noun while ghayra serves as the object of 'do.'
The question is a censure and affirmative reminder, answering their plea: they were granted sufficient life to repent and heed guidance, so their request is rebuked.

words: أَوَلَمْ نُعَمِّرْكُم مَّا يَتَذَكَّرُ فِيهِ مَن تَذَكَّرَ
view: The allotted time sufficed for any willing person to reflect, heed the evidence, amend conduct, and repent; longer life strengthens the rebuke.
The lifespan itself is evidence against the damned and leaves disbelief without excuse; God's postponement allowed reflection, while after resurrection the opportunity has closed.
Questioning people for their conduct and citing their lifetime as evidence imply that they possessed choice and capacity to act.
God supplied both inward ability to reflect and external guidance; failure arose from neglect of revelation, not absence of recited guidance.
The stated sufficient term applies to those who die after puberty; those who die before maturity receive more lenient treatment.
Taʿmīr means extending a person's life.
The sufficient span starts at puberty or maturity, the first stage of discernment and responsible reflection.
One reported threshold is seventeen years.
One reported threshold is eighteen years; some reports describe an eighteen-year-old present or the person to whom the rebuke applied when the verse was revealed.
One reported threshold is twenty years.
One reported threshold is forty years, when understanding reaches maturity; al-Ṭabarī prefers it over sixty partly from concern about a transmitter in the sixty report, and others also call it sound.
Another reported threshold is forty-six years.
Another reported threshold is fifty years; poetry depicts fifty as advanced age and near death.
One prominent interpretation sets the sufficient lifetime at sixty years. Al-Wāḥidī and Ibn Kathīr prefer it on Prophetic-report grounds; Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds it apt, while al-Ṭabarī prefers forty.
One report treats any age from twenty through sixty as a sufficient period.
Another view sets the period at seventy, the last time for reflection before senility.

Prophetic reports say that reaching sixty, or in some transmissions sixty or seventy, removes a person's excuse because God has granted ample life and warning; al-Bukhārī titled a chapter accordingly, and Ibn Kathīr accepts the hadith through several routes.
Reports say a caller on Judgment Day summons those who reached sixty and cites this verse; Ibn Kathīr questions one route because of Ibrāhīm ibn al-Faḍl.

Reports place most of the Prophet's community's lifespans and deaths between sixty and seventy, with few exceeding that; Ibn Kathīr calls one chain weak, while al-Tirmidhī calls another ḥasan gharīb and al-Bazzār flags a weak transmitter.
A report gives the community's lifespan as fifty to sixty years and invokes mercy on those reaching seventy or eighty.
Physicians cited by Ibn Kathīr propose a natural lifespan of 120 years, with growth until sixty and decline afterward; a poem depicts the loss of youthful pleasure at sixty.
The Prophet's lifespan is most often given as sixty-three years, though reports also say sixty and sixty-five.
Reports describe people turning more wholly toward worship and the hereafter at forty; a poem warns that one still without restraint at forty has chosen his path.
A daily and nightly caller reportedly warns at forty that harvest nears, at sixty to account for deeds, and at seventy to face reckoning.
ʿAbd al-Qādir tells a young penitent that God preserved and drew him near despite earlier estrangement, and an old penitent that pardon and delay remain open to return despite displeasure in old age.
A Persian couplet contrasts young people hastening toward spiritual gain with the hindrance of old age; death's hidden time means no age is safe.
Mā denotes a period or indefinite span of time in which a person can remember; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn ʿĀshūr describe a temporal expression.

One parse treats mā as a temporal verbal noun meaning the duration of remembering; al-Samīn rejects it because fīhi refers back to mā unless such a verbal noun functions as a noun. Al-Ālūsī records the same objection and a possible implied referent.
Treating mā as a negative particle is rejected as untenable in wording and meaning.
The common reading has mā yatadhakkaru fīhi man tadhakkar; al-Aʿmash reads an assimilated form from idhkar, with a linking hamza reportedly pronounced in connected recitation.
'The warner came to you' coordinates with the affirmative sense of 'Did We not give you life?' as 'We gave you life, and the warner came'; another parse coordinates with its form.
The warner is Muhammad, the messenger whose warning makes people responsible; identifying him stresses the warning aspect of his mission, and some cite other verses calling him a warner.
note: The competing identifications are the Qur'an, all prophets, gray hair, reason and signs of mortality.

view: The singular warner is generic for prophets: each prophet warned his contemporaries, with Muhammad warning later people.
The warner is the Qurʾān or revealed scripture.
The warner is gray hair, a visible sign of advancing age and approaching death; poetry and a saying about each white hair reinforce this usage.
note: Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this apt but says binding proof comes through scriptural warning.

view: Gray hair warns that youth and its play have passed, prompting preparation for death.
A report says Abraham was the first descendant of Adam to gray; God called gray hair dignity in this world and light in the next, and Abraham asked for more.
A reported hadith says God dislikes an elderly man whose hair has not turned gray.
The warner may be fever, which heralds death.
The warner may be the deaths of relatives, friends, or neighbors, repeatedly reminding survivors of their own departure; poetry illustrates the point.
The warner may be mature reason, by which one discerns reality and moral difference and prepares for the hereafter.
Extreme old age itself may be the warning.
Nadhīr can mean a warning rather than a particular warning-bearer.
If nadhīr denotes Muhammad it is an active participle; if it denotes gray hair it is better read as a verbal noun. Its singular form suits the immediate context.
Every sign of impending departure from life can count as a warner calling for heedfulness.
Long life and the messengers together were evidence against them; messengers and books supplied warning beyond what reason alone established.
One explanation takes the warning as the subsidiary branches of religious rulings.
An alternate recitation reads the warning term in the plural, al-nudhur, instead of the singular nadhīr.
The command orders them to taste Hell's punishment, with remorse and continuing torment; its fāʾ makes that punishment the consequence of their failure to heed their lifetime and the warning.
The imperative 'taste' humiliates the damned and signals enduring punishment; its object, punishment, is omitted.
The wrongdoers here are unbelievers and polytheists who wronged themselves through disbelief and idolatry.
Wrongdoing violates another's due; its gravest form is shirk, which affronts God's oneness and harms the self by bringing punishment.
No one can defend or rescue the wrongdoers from God's punishment, restraints, and chains; their former allies and idols cannot help.
One theological reading concludes that major sinners receive no intercession.
Al-Rāzī's preferred broad reading excludes all help, from God or anyone else.
An alternative says the wrongdoer's compounded ignorance, mistaking falsehood for truth, leaves him without beneficial knowledge in the afterlife.
The singular helper fits their situation after despair of human allies and idols, when they hope only for God; other passages depict earlier expectations of idol-help.
Their lack of helpers follows from turning away from God and the help He sent during worldly life.
The denial of help may continue the rebuke to the damned and end hope of rescue, or it may be an independent conclusion for listeners applying to every wrongdoer.
Min naṣīr may be a subject governed by the preposition or a topic whose predicate is the preceding prepositional phrase.
Because aiding oppression violates justice, the community should restrain wrongdoing; a Prophetic report explains that helping an unjust person means stopping his injustice.
In an ishārī reading, people sleep in worldly heedlessness and wake fully after death and resurrection, when they perceive the punishment they taste.
The preceding comparison of believers and unbelievers leads into the contrast of God's power with idols and the outcome of disbelief.
Without faith and righteous deeds, wealth and children increase ruin; worldly possessions and family are vulnerable, whereas the faithful receive manifold reward and enduring safety in the chambers.
In a neighboring passage, some read bayyinah singular, pointing to scripture or what the Prophet brought; others read bayyināt plural for each prophet's proof or several forms of scriptural evidence.
In a neighboring passage, maqt means hatred, and the hated person may be called mamqūt or maqīt.
The pronoun refers to the disbelievers in the preceding verse; the clause continues the account of their being in Hell rather than serving as a circumstantial clause.
One legal application says Hajj may be delayed while completion remains likely; sudden death incurs no sin, whereas a clear warning that delay risks missing it makes postponement impermissible.
Masrūq cautions those who reach forty to be mindful of God; reaching sixty nears death and calls for repentance, humility, and preparation to meet God.
The claim that those blind in worldly life remain blind in the afterlife explains the futility of their request to return.
Proof may be called sulṭān because authority or power provides aid.
